kinds.description:
AWSAccount is an AWS account your tenant works in. You add one for each account you operate, which is what tells Wayfinder the account exists before any credential for it does — so you can see and pick it while setting the rest up.

Its name is the AWS account ID, e.g. "123456789012", so an account is the same object however it is reached and a reference to it can never come to mean a different real account. Give it a display name to say what it is for.

It grants no access of its own: an external identity naming this account is what lets Wayfinder act in it. It records only facts about the account and never changes state, so it has no status.

spec.description: AWSAccountSpec says what to call an AWS account. The account ID itself is the object's name.

displayName.description: DisplayName is an editable, human-facing name for this account that explains what it is for (e.g. "Example - dev"). Lists and pickers show it in place of the account ID.

kinds.description:
AzureSubscription is an Azure subscription your tenant works in. You add one for each subscription you operate, which is what tells Wayfinder the subscription exists before any credential for it does — so you can see and pick it while setting the rest up.

Its name is the subscription ID, e.g. "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", so a subscription is the same object however it is reached and a reference to it can never come to mean a different real subscription. Give it a display name to say what it is for.

It grants no access of its own: an external identity naming this subscription is what lets Wayfinder act in it. It records only facts about the subscription and never changes state, so it has no status.

spec.description: AzureSubscriptionSpec records what to call an Azure subscription and which tenant it lives in. The subscription ID itself is the object's name.

displayName.description: DisplayName is an editable, human-facing name for this subscription that explains what it is for (e.g. "Example - dev"). Lists and pickers show it in place of the subscription ID.

tenantID.description: TenantID is the Azure tenant this subscription belongs to, e.g. "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111". A subscription belongs to exactly one tenant, so it is recorded here rather than on each identity that reaches it — an identity created against this subscription takes it from here. It cannot be changed once set.

kinds.description:
GCPProject is a Google Cloud project your tenant works in. You add one for each project you operate, which is what tells Wayfinder the project exists before any credential for it does — so you can see and pick it while setting the rest up.

Its name is the project ID, e.g. "example-project", so a project is the same object however it is reached and a reference to it can never come to mean a different real project. Give it a display name to say what it is for.

It grants no access of its own: an external identity naming this project is what lets Wayfinder act in it. It records only facts about the project and never changes state, so it has no status.

spec.description: GCPProjectSpec records what to call a Google Cloud project and the number Google assigned it. The project ID itself is the object's name.

displayName.description: DisplayName is an editable, human-facing name for this project that explains what it is for (e.g. "Example - dev"). Lists and pickers show it in place of the project ID.

projectNumber.description: ProjectNumber is the numerical ID Google assigned the project when it was created, e.g. "123456789012". It is permanent, distinct from the project ID held as this object's name, and required to reach the project from outside Google Cloud — so it is recorded here rather than on each identity, and an identity created against this project takes it from here. It cannot be changed once set.

kinds.description:
CloudResource is a single deployment of a CloudResourcePlan into a cloud account, provisioned with Terraform/OpenTofu from the plan's template and the inputs given here. It may be infrastructure — a database, a storage bucket, a network — or an application workload running on a managed cloud runtime such as Cloud Run, Lambda or Azure Container Apps.

Its status carries what the deployment produced: the outputs applications consume, the workload identity they use to reach it, the permissions that identity can be granted, and where its Terraform/OpenTofu state is kept. Create one directly, or let a stack instance create it as part of deploying an application.

identityRef.description: IdentityRef references the ExternalIdentity Wayfinder authenticates with, for a cloud or service destination, e.g. "my-workspace/aws-nonprod". A kubernetes destination uses clusterRoles instead.

clusterRoles.description: ClusterRoles names the Kubernetes cluster roles anything deployed through this target is bound to, for a kubernetes destination — the access it deploys with. Each entry names a role the cluster owner has allocated to your workspace and the scope to bind it at, e.g. {"clusterRoleName": "cluster-admin", "roleBindingType": "Cluster"}. Left unset, the cluster's default deployment role is used where it has one, and at least one role must be named where it does not. A cloud or service destination uses identityRef instead.

roleBindingType.description: RoleBindingType is the scope to bind at: Namespace (the default) binds in the target's namespace, Cluster binds cluster-wide.

planRef.description: PlanRef is the cloud resource plan, and optionally the plan version, to provision from, e.g. "aws-s3-bucket@3" for a plan shared across the tenant or "team-payments/orders-db@2" for one owned by a workspace. A plan from Wayfinder's catalogue is referenced by the copy you installed. The version actually used for the most recent deployment is reported in status.

stackInstanceRef.description: StackInstanceRef is the stack instance this resource was deployed as part of, when it was created by deploying an application rather than on its own. The stack instance's name and environment are available to the plan's templates.

name.description: Name is the object name of the referenced stack instance

workspace.description: Workspace identifies the workspace in which this item exists. If empty, assume the same workspace as the object holding the reference.

environment.description: Environment identifies the environment in which this item exists.

cloud.description: Cloud is the cloud provider this resource is provisioned in, e.g. "aws". It must agree with the cloud named by destination. Deprecated: derivable from destination, and becomes so in the next release.

dependsOn.description: DependsOn lists other cloud resources this one depends on. Each entry gives the dependency a logical name, which the plan's templates use to read that resource's outputs, and which workloadIdentity.accessTo uses to request permissions on it. Wayfinder provisions dependencies first.

items.description: DependsOnResource names another cloud resource this one depends on, under a logical name used to refer to it.

name.description: Name is the logical name this dependency is referred to by, e.g. "database". Templates read its outputs under this name, and workloadIdentity.accessTo requests permissions on it by this name.

cloudResourceRef.description: CloudResourceRef is the cloud resource being depended on.

name.description: Name is the object name of the referenced item

workspace.description: Workspace identifies the workspace in which this item exists. If empty, assume the same workspace as the object holding the reference.

environment.description: Environment identifies the environment in which this item exists.

region.description: Region is the cloud region to provision this resource in, e.g. "eu-west-2" (AWS) or "westeurope" (Azure). It must agree with the region named by destination. Deprecated: derivable from destination, and becomes so in the next release.

inputs.description: Inputs are the values supplied to the plan's inputs. Each may be a literal or a template expression, e.g. "${{ .Vars.dbName }}" to read from the variable and secret hierarchy (tenant > workspace > environment), and the plan decides which inputs are accepted and which are required.

values.description: Values are named input values matching the plan's ValueDefinitions. May contain template expressions (e.g. "${{ .Vars.name }}", "${{ .Secrets.key }}"). Resolved when Wayfinder applies the configuration — secret values are never stored here.

items.description: TemplatedInput is a named input value, potentially containing template expressions.

name.description: Name matches a ValueDefinition on the associated plan.

value.description: Value is a literal value or template expression, resolved at reconciliation time. Stored as json.RawMessage so non-string types (numbers, bools) survive YAML round-trips without forced quoting. Template expressions like "${{ .Vars.x }}" are stored as JSON strings.

workloadIdentity.description: WorkloadIdentity requests a cloud identity that applications can assume to reach this resource. It is only accepted when the referenced plan declares workload identity support.

cloudResourceName.description: CloudResourceName is the name to give the identity in the cloud account, e.g. "orders-db-reader". Leave it blank to derive the name from the cloud resource's own name.

identityOnly.description: IdentityOnly creates the identity with no permissions attached, leaving you to grant them yourself in the cloud account. In AWS the IAM role is created but no inline or attached policies are managed after creation; in Azure the user-assigned managed identity is created but no role definitions or role assignments are made.

accessTo.description: AccessTo requests permissions on other cloud resources this one depends on, so an application using this identity can reach them too.

items.description: CloudResourceAccessTo grants this resource's workload identity a named set of permissions on one of the cloud resources it depends on.

depName.description: DepName is the logical name of the dependency to be granted access to. It must name a single entry in this resource's dependsOn list.

consumptionPolicy.description: ConsumptionPolicy is the name of the permission set to grant, e.g. "read-only". It must be one of the consumption policies published by the plan the dependency was provisioned from.

terraform.description: Terraform holds per-resource overrides of the Terraform/OpenTofu configuration the plan defines.

tfVarsTemplate.description: TFVarsTemplate is a template rendered into an extra tfvars file applied on top of the plan's own configuration, so this resource can override or extend it, e.g. "instance_class = "${{ .Inputs.size }}"". The rendered result is reported in status.

kinds.description:
CloudResourcePlan is a reusable, versioned Terraform/OpenTofu template that developers can provision cloud resources from without writing Terraform themselves. It provisions either infrastructure — a database, a storage bucket, a network — or an application runtime such as Cloud Run, Lambda or Azure Container Apps.

A plan declares the inputs it accepts and the outputs it produces, the Terraform files and modules that build the resource, and optionally a workload identity for applications to assume along with the named sets of permissions ("consumption policies") that identity can be granted. Published to the catalogue, it becomes a self-service option: each deployment of it is a CloudResource.

Plans are versioned, so a new version can be published without disturbing resources already provisioned from an earlier one, and can be defined by Wayfinder, by a tenant for all its workspaces, or by a single workspace.

spec.description: CloudResourcePlanSpec defines a plan for a cloud resource.

cloud.description: Cloud refers to the cloud provider of the resource (azure, gcp, aws).

resourceType.description: ResourceType classifies this plan as either a runtime (a platform for applications to run on) or a dependency (an application dependency such as a data store, queue, or other infrastructure). The catalogue uses it to help developers find the right kind of plan.

enumDocs.description: Indicates the plan provisions a platform for applications to run on (e.g. a managed runtime, FaaS, container host).
Indicates the plan provisions an application dependency — data stores, queues, networking, or other infrastructure that applications consume.

category.description: Category is a cloud-agnostic taxonomy entry drawn from a curated industry-standard list, e.g. "compute", "storage" or "databases". It lets developers browse and search the catalogue by category.

description.description: Description is a short summary of what this plan provisions, shown in the catalogue, e.g. "A PostgreSQL database with automated backups".

inputs.description: Inputs are the values this plan accepts from whoever provisions a resource from it, and determine what a developer may configure. Each definition gives the input a name, a type, whether it is required and any default.

items.description: ValueDefinition defines the shape of an input/output/data value

name.description: Name of the variable

description.description: Description iof the value

secret.description: Secret indicates if the value is a secret and should be protected

type.description: Type is the type of the value

enumDocs.description: Is a string type
Is a number type (integer or floating point)
Is a boolean type
Is a list type of strings
Is a list type of numbers
Is a list type of booleans
Is a map type of strings
Is a map type of numbers
Is a map type of booleans
Is an arbitrary JSON type, used to represent any complex input/output that isn't better represented by the other types. Note that no validation is possible for a plain JSON input.

Is a reference to an ExternalIdentity, naming the credential an outbound call authenticates with. The value is the identity's name and the scope it lives at ("my-identity", "my-workspace/my-identity" or "my-workspace/my-env/my-identity"), never credential material itself. Supplying a value resolves it: the identity must exist, you must be allowed to use it for what is calling, and its own kind must be one the definition's identityTypes accepts. A value naming an identity that fails any of those is refused when it is supplied, rather than failing when the call runs. It may only be declared where a definition is able to load an identity. It is refused on a CloudResourcePlan's inputs and outputs, a KubeResourcePlan's inputs, a stack definition's vars, an IntegrationDefinition's paramDefs, and a repo template's inputs, all of which would otherwise receive the reference as a plain string.

Is a reference to a CodeRepo, naming the repository an AI agent works on. The value names the repository as its provider does, "github.com/OWNER/REPO" (e.g. "github.com/appvia/wayfinder"), never a URL or a git credential. Use it on an AI agent's input where the repository is not fixed when the agent is written: the input sets how much of the repository the agent needs (repoAccess) and the branch prefix for its changes (repoBranchPrefix), and whoever starts the conversation supplies the repository. The conversation's spec.sourceContext is built from the value they supply. Supplying a value resolves it: the repository must exist, and the grant in its usableBy must cover the access the input asks for. That grant is checked against the person supplying the repository, not against whoever wrote the agent. The agent is checked separately, against the same repository, when the conversation is created. It may only be declared where a definition is able to load a repository and check that grant. It is refused on a CloudResourcePlan's and a KubeResourcePlan's inputs and outputs, a stack definition's vars, an IntegrationDefinition's paramDefs, and a repo template's inputs: each of those passes its values through as text to Terraform, a Helm chart, a rendered manifest or a scaffolded file, where the reference is only a plain string and no grant over the repository is checked.

optional.description: Optional is true when no value need be supplied: the object declaring it can be saved, and switched on where it has a switch, without one. An unanswered optional value reads as its defaultValue when one is set, and as nothing otherwise. Whether whoever uses the object may supply it later is for that object to say.

minimum.description: Minimum is the minimum numerical value of the variable if a number/float

maximum.description: Maximum is the maximum numerical value of the variable if a number/float

minLength.description: MinLength is the minimum number or length of the variable if a string

maxLength.description: MaxLength is the maximum number or length of the variable if a string

minItems.description: MinItems is the minimum number of items in the variable if a list or map

maxItems.description: MaxItems is the maximum number of items in the variable if a list or map

pattern.description: Pattern is the pattern of the variable if a string. For list(string) and map(string), this is applied to each individual value in the list or map.

enum.description: Enum is the list of valid values for a string or number (or the values of lists/maps of those types). Ignored for other types.

requiredKeys.description: RequiredKeys is the list of required keys for a map variable. Ignored for other types.

refType.description: RefType describes that this value is a reference to another Wayfinder resource. When set, the value is validated to be the name of an existing resource of the given kind, optionally filtered by field constraints.

kind.description: Kind is the Wayfinder resource kind being referenced (e.g. "ExternalIdentity", "CodeRepo")

filter.description: Filter is an optional set of dot-path field matchers on the referenced resource. Keys are dot-paths (e.g. "spec.cloud"), values are the expected string match. All entries must match (AND semantics).

identityTypes.description: IdentityTypes lists the ExternalIdentity types this input accepts, e.g. ["BearerToken"] for an API that authenticates with a bearer token, or ["BasicAuth", "BearerToken"] where either will do. A value naming an identity of any other type is refused when it is supplied, rather than failing when the call runs. Leaving it empty accepts any identity type that can authenticate an outbound call. It may be set only on type=externalidentity, and is refused on every other type.

repoAccess.description: RepoAccess is how much of the repository the agent needs: "read" to clone and read it, "propose" to also commit to a fresh branch and open a pull request, or "proposeWorkflows" to also change the repository's CI workflow definitions. When empty, Wayfinder uses "read". Whoever supplies a repository must themselves be granted at least this much of it, and so must the agent, or the conversation is refused when it is created. It may be set only on type=coderepo, and is refused on every other type.

repoBranchPrefix.description: RepoBranchPrefix is prepended to the name of the branch the agent's changes are committed to, e.g. "wayfinder-ai/cost-control/". When empty, branches are prefixed "wayfinder-ai/". Set it so branch protection or CODEOWNERS rules in the repository match every branch this agent opens; whoever starts the conversation cannot change it. It may be set only on type=coderepo, and is refused on every other type.

terraform.description: Terraform is the Terraform/OpenTofu configuration that provisions the resource — the files to render, the modules to fetch and any extra providers they need.

modules.description: Modules is an optional list of Terraform modules to fetch. Each module must be referenced in file templates, e.g.: source = ${{ .Modules.NAME.Source | quote }} Version must be referenced in file templates if using a registry source, e.g.: version = ${{ .Modules.NAME.Version | quote }}

items.description: ModuleReference defines a reference to an external Terraform module.

name.description: Name to use to reference this module in file templates, e.g.: source = ${{ .Modules.NAME.Source | quote }}

source.description:
Source is the Terraform module source URL. Wayfinder supports user-friendly URL formats that are automatically normalized for Terraform compatibility.

Supported formats: - Registry format: `terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws` or `registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/consul/aws` - GitHub/GitLab shorthand: `github.com/org/repo` or `gitlab.com/org/repo` - Git URLs: `git::https://github.com/org/repo.git` - HTTPS URLs: `https://github.com/org/repo` (automatically converted to git:: format)

Subdirectories can be specified with double-slash: `https://github.com/org/repo//modules/vpc`

Reference in file templates, e.g.: source = ${{ .Modules.NAME.Source | quote }}

version.description: Version is the module version or git ref to use. For git sources, this is appended as `?ref={version}`. For registry sources, this is used in file templates, e.g.: version = ${{ .Modules.NAME.Version | quote }}

externalIdentityRef.description: ExternalIdentityRef references an ExternalIdentity carrying the credentials for fetching this module from a private source. It must be a BasicAuth (username/password registries and private git over HTTP, including a GitHub token as the password) or a BearerToken (token-authenticated Module Registry Protocol registries) identity whose service host matches the module source host. Leave empty for public modules.

files.description: Files is the list of .tf file templates that define the Terraform configuration. Each file is rendered using the template context and written to the working directory before terraform init/plan/apply.

items.description: TerraformFile defines a Terraform file to be generated from a template.

name.description: Name is the filename for the generated Terraform file. Should end in .tf (e.g., "main.tf", "outputs.tf", "variables.tf"). Must be unique within the list of files.

template.description: Template is a Go template that renders to valid Terraform HCL. The template has access to the standard Wayfinder template context including .Inputs, .Components, .Outputs, .Cloud, .Workspace, etc.

additionalProviders.description: AdditionalProviders is a list of additional Terraform providers needed beyond the default cloud provider (aws/azure/gcp based on spec.cloud).

additionalRegionalProviders.description:
AdditionalRegionalProviders declares additional regional aliases of the cloud's providers — needed for AWS/GCP services that are pinned to a specific region regardless of the CloudAccount's default region (e.g. ACM certificates for CloudFront which must live in us-east-1).

Wayfinder generates aliased `provider "<name>"` blocks in the managed provider.tf alongside the default block; plan templates reference them as `provider = <name>.<alias>` (e.g. `provider = aws.us_east_1`).

Supported only on aws and gcp clouds — azurerm doesn't take a region at the provider level.

items.description: RegionalProviderAlias declares a regional alias of one of the cloud's Terraform providers. Wayfinder owns rendering — plan templates must not include `provider "..."` blocks themselves.

alias.description: Alias is the HCL alias label used to reference this provider in plan templates (e.g. alias "us_east_1" is referenced as `provider = aws.us_east_1`). Must be a valid HCL identifier: lowercase, start with a letter, contain only letters/numbers/underscores. Must be unique per provider within the list.

region.description: Region is the cloud region this alias pins to. Required.

provider.description: Provider is the Terraform provider name to alias. Optional — defaults to the cloud's default provider (aws for spec.cloud=aws, google for spec.cloud=gcp). When set, must be either the default provider or one of the providers listed in spec.terraform.additionalProviders.

consumptionPolicies.description: ConsumptionPolicies are the named sets of permissions that can be granted on resources provisioned from this plan, e.g. "read-only". An application asks for one by name and its workload identity is granted the corresponding cloud permissions.

items.description: ConsumptionPolicy is a named set of permissions that can be granted to an application's workload identity so it can use a resource provisioned from this plan.

name.description: Name is the name applications ask for this permission set by, e.g. "read-only", "read-write", "admin" or "backup-access".

kinds.description:
CloudResourceStateStore says where the state that Wayfinder keeps for cloud resources is stored in your own cloud. Every cloud resource is provisioned through Terraform/OpenTofu, which records what it created in a state file; this resource names the bucket, container or storage account those files live in, either as a naming convention per cloud that covers every account in it or as an explicit location for a particular destination.

A resource's state is kept in the cloud it deploys to, so a tenant using more than one cloud gives a convention for each: state for an AWS account goes to the Amazon S3 convention, state for an Azure subscription to the Azure one, and so on.

It is set at tenant, workspace or environment level, under the well-known name "default". The nearest one wins and is merged field by field over the levels above it, so a team can adjust a single field — for example a prefix — without restating the whole configuration. What a lower level is allowed to change is controlled by the override policy on the tenant-level resource.

Changing this configuration only affects cloud resources created afterwards: each resource remembers the location it was first given, so existing state is never moved or lost.

spec.description: CloudResourceStateStoreSpec describes where cloud resource state is stored: a naming convention per cloud that resolves to a location for any account in that cloud, plus explicit locations for individual destinations that do not follow it.

awsS3.description: AWSS3 is the naming convention for state belonging to AWS accounts, held in Amazon S3 buckets. Give it if you deploy to AWS; the cloud a resource deploys to picks the convention used.

bucketTemplate.description: BucketTemplate is the name of the S3 bucket, written as a template so that one convention can serve every cloud account, e.g. "acme-tfstate-{{ .Cloud.AccountID }}". Only the cloud account being set up may be referenced: "{{ .Cloud.AccountID }}" for its identifier and "{{ .Cloud.Cloud }}" for its cloud. A name with no template in it puts every account's state in one bucket. It is required whenever this convention is given at tenant level; a workspace or environment leaves it out to inherit the level above.

region.description: Region is the AWS region the bucket lives in, e.g. "eu-west-2". Leave it empty to use the region of the cloud account the resource is deployed to.

prefix.description: Prefix is prepended to the path of every state file in the bucket, e.g. "acme/", so state can share a bucket with other content.

azureRM.description: AzureRM is the naming convention for state belonging to Azure subscriptions, held in Azure storage accounts. Give it if you deploy to Azure; the cloud a resource deploys to picks the convention used.

storageAccountTemplate.description: StorageAccountTemplate is the name of the storage account, written as a template so that one convention can serve every subscription, e.g. "acmetfstate{{ .Cloud.AccountID }}". Only the cloud account being set up may be referenced: "{{ .Cloud.AccountID }}" for its identifier and "{{ .Cloud.Cloud }}" for its cloud. It is required whenever this convention is given at tenant level; a workspace or environment leaves it out to inherit the level above.

container.description: Container is the blob container within the storage account that holds the state files, e.g. "tfstate". It is required whenever this convention is given at tenant level; a workspace or environment leaves it out to inherit the level above.

resourceGroup.description: ResourceGroup is the Azure resource group the storage account belongs to, e.g. "acme-platform-rg".

prefix.description: Prefix is prepended to the path of every state file in the container, e.g. "acme/", so state can share a container with other content.

gcpCloudStorage.description: GCPCloudStorage is the naming convention for state belonging to GCP projects, held in Google Cloud Storage buckets. Give it if you deploy to GCP; the cloud a resource deploys to picks the convention used.

bucketTemplate.description: BucketTemplate is the name of the Cloud Storage bucket, written as a template so that one convention can serve every project, e.g. "acme-tfstate-{{ .Cloud.AccountID }}". Only the cloud account being set up may be referenced: "{{ .Cloud.AccountID }}" for its identifier and "{{ .Cloud.Cloud }}" for its cloud. It is required whenever this convention is given at tenant level; a workspace or environment leaves it out to inherit the level above.

location.description: Location is the Cloud Storage location the bucket lives in, e.g. "europe-west2". Leave it empty to use the location of the cloud account the resource is deployed to.

prefix.description: Prefix is prepended to the path of every state file in the bucket, e.g. "acme/", so state can share a bucket with other content.

destinations.description: Destinations gives explicit state locations for individual destinations, keyed by the whole cloud account a resource deploys to, e.g. "aws:123456789012" — no region, because state is kept once per account rather than per region. An entry replaces the naming convention for that destination and is used exactly as written, and the location it states must match the key's cloud. Entries are merged by key across tenant, workspace and environment levels, so a lower level can add or replace one destination's location without affecting the rest.

values.description: StateStoreLocation is the explicit state location for one destination. Its values are used exactly as written — no templates — and take the place of the naming convention for that destination. Fill in exactly one sub-block, matching the cloud of the destination it is keyed by.

awsS3.description: AWSS3 is the Amazon S3 location holding this destination's state.

bucket.description: Bucket is the name of the S3 bucket, e.g. "acme-tfstate-prod".

region.description: Region is the AWS region the bucket lives in, e.g. "eu-west-2". Leave it empty to use the region of the cloud account the resource is deployed to.

prefix.description: Prefix is prepended to the path of every state file in the bucket, e.g. "tf/".

overridePolicy.description: OverridePolicy controls which parts of this configuration a workspace or environment may set for itself. It is read from the tenant-level resource only; setting it at a lower level has no effect. With no tenant-level resource, no lower-level configuration is accepted at all.

default.description: Default is what happens to a field the allow list does not name. It defaults to "Deny", so a workspace or environment may set only what is explicitly allowed.

enumDocs.description: Rejects any field not named in the allow list.
Accepts any field, making the allow list unnecessary.

allow.description: Allow lists the fields a workspace or environment may set, each as a dot-separated path into the spec, e.g. "awsS3.prefix".

kinds.description: DNSZone represents a hosted DNS zone for a domain in AWS Route 53, Azure DNS, or Google Cloud DNS. Wayfinder creates the zone in the cloud account you point it at, publishes its authoritative nameservers, and — where you name a parent zone that Wayfinder also manages — sets up and checks the delegation between the two. Clusters and applications draw their host names from the zone's entry templates, so deployments get working DNS without anyone editing records by hand. A zone can also be marked unmanaged, in which case Wayfinder only verifies it exists and uses it as a delegation parent.

spec.description: DNSZoneSpec defines the desired configuration of a DNS zone to be provisioned.

parentZone.description: ParentZone should be set to make this zone a child of another zone managed by Wayfinder, e.g. a zone for "dev.example.com" whose parent holds "example.com". Setting this allows Wayfinder to automatically manage the delegation of this zone.

workspace.description: Workspace identifies the workspace in which this item exists.

environment.description: Environment identifies the environment in which this item exists.

name.description: Name is the object name of the referenced item

description.description: Description provides an optional human-readable description and should be used to provide context to users about what this zone should be used for.

provider.description: Provider is the cloud provider hosting this zone: "aws" (Route 53), "azure" (Azure DNS), or "gcp" (Google Cloud DNS).

destination.description: Destination is the place this target names, e.g. "aws:123456789012:eu-west-2", "k8s:my-workspace/dev/my-cluster:my-namespace" or "srv:vault.internal.corp:8443".

identityRef.description: IdentityRef references the ExternalIdentity Wayfinder authenticates with, for a cloud or service destination, e.g. "my-workspace/aws-nonprod". A kubernetes destination uses clusterRoles instead.

clusterRoles.description: ClusterRoles names the Kubernetes cluster roles anything deployed through this target is bound to, for a kubernetes destination — the access it deploys with. Each entry names a role the cluster owner has allocated to your workspace and the scope to bind it at, e.g. {"clusterRoleName": "cluster-admin", "roleBindingType": "Cluster"}. Left unset, the cluster's default deployment role is used where it has one, and at least one role must be named where it does not. A cloud or service destination uses identityRef instead.

items.description: TargetClusterRole names a Kubernetes ClusterRole the deployment identity is bound to, and the scope it is bound at.

clusterRoleName.description: ClusterRoleName is the name of the ClusterRole in the target cluster, chosen from the roles the cluster owner has allocated to your workspace, e.g. "cluster-admin".

roleBindingType.description: RoleBindingType is the scope to bind at: Namespace (the default) binds in the target's namespace, Cluster binds cluster-wide.

Creates ClusterRoleBindings for cluster-wide access

domain.description: Domain is the fully-qualified domain name this zone is authoritative for, e.g. "dev.example.com".

privateZone.description: PrivateZone indicates that this is a private DNS zone, resolvable only from the networks listed in the provider details, if applicable for the provider.

providerDetails.description: ProviderDetails carries the extra settings needed by a particular DNS provider, such as the networks a private zone is resolvable from.

type.description: Type selects which provider block applies: AWS, Azure, or GCP.

roleBindingType.description: RoleBindingType is the scope to bind at: Namespace (the default) binds in the target's namespace, Cluster binds cluster-wide.

Creates ClusterRoleBindings for cluster-wide access

vpcID.description: VPCID is the ID of the AWS VPC to associate the private hosted zone with, e.g. "vpc-1234abc0" or "vpc-1234567890abcdef0".

region.description: Region is the AWS region in which the VPC exists, e.g. "eu-west-2". It must agree with the region named by destination.

gcp.description: GCP holds parameters specific to a GCP DNS zone. Present only if type is GCP.

privateZoneVPCs.description: PrivateZoneVPCs is a list of VPC network IDs a private Google Cloud DNS zone should be resolvable from, e.g. "projects/my-project/global/networks/my-network".

azure.description: Azure holds parameters specific to an Azure DNS zone. Present only if type is Azure.

region.description: Region is the Azure region the resource group holding this zone is created in, e.g. "uksouth". Resource groups are regional in Azure, so a region is required for an Azure DNS zone even though the zone itself is global.

resourceGroup.description: ResourceGroup identifies an existing resource group to place this DNS zone in, e.g. "my-dns-rg". Leave it unset to have a new resource group created for the zone.

privateZoneVNetIDs.description: PrivateZoneVNetIDs is a list of virtual network IDs a private Azure DNS zone should be resolvable from, e.g. "/subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourceGroups/my-rg/providers/Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/my-vnet". The identity used for this zone must be allowed the 'join' action on the virtual networks listed here.

unmanaged.description: Unmanaged should be set to true to indicate that this zone should not be built or deleted by Wayfinder, but should be verified to exist in the specified DNS provider and, thus, will be usable as a parent zone.

clusterPackageDNSEntryTemplate.description:
ClusterPackageDNSEntryTemplate defines how the 'getDNSEntry' template function works when templating cluster-scoped packages (i.e. those used on a cluster plan).

The available template variables are: * {{ .Cluster }} - name of the cluster (max 10 characters alphanumeric) * {{ .Package }} - name of the package * {{ .Prefix }} - any prefix supplied to the 'getDNSEntry' template function * {{ .Domain }} - the domain of this zone - the provided template MUST end with this

Example: "{{ if .Prefix }}{{ .Prefix }}-{{ end }}{{ .Package }}.{{ .Cluster }}.{{ .Domain }}"

appDNSEntryTemplate.description:
AppDNSEntryTemplate defines how the 'getDNSEntry' template function works when templating application deployments (i.e. those requested through Wayfinder.yaml / 'wf up' / 'wf deploy')

The available template variables are: * {{ .Cluster }} - name of the cluster (max 10 characters alphanumeric) * {{ .Stack }} - name of the stack (i.e. Wayfinder.yaml 'name', max 32 characters alphanumeric with - and . allowed) * {{ .StackInstance }} - name of the stack instance (max 32 characters alphanumeric with - and . allowed) * {{ .StackInstanceClean }} - name of the stack instance with any stack name prefix or suffix removed (max 32 characters alphanumeric with - and . allowed) * {{ .MultiTenant }} - true if the stack is in a different workspace to the cluster * {{ .Prefix }} - any prefix supplied to the 'getDNSEntry' template function * {{ .Domain }} - the domain of this zone - the provided template MUST end with this

Examples: * Shared DNS zone for all apps/envs:
  "{{ if .Prefix }}{{ .Prefix }}-{{ end }}{{ .StackInstance }}.{{ .Domain }}"
* Dedicated DNS zone for a single app environment (e.g. your production vanity domain):
  "{{ if .Prefix }}{{ .Prefix }}.{{ end }}{{ .Domain }}"

kinds.description:
AIAgent is a configured AI agent: the instructions it works to, the models it may run on, the tools and MCP servers it can call, and the durable memories it keeps between runs. Starting a conversation with an agent is how AI-powered work is done in Wayfinder, whether that is the general assistant answering a question or a specialised agent authoring and testing a resource plan.

Wayfinder ships a set of built-in agents, referenced as "wayfinder/NAME". A tenant can also define its own, at tenant, workspace or environment scope, and reference those by name.

spec.description: AIAgentSpec defines the desired configuration of an AI agent: how it is prompted, what it may call, and what a conversation with it must supply.

systemPrompt.description: SystemPrompt is the standing instruction the agent works to. It may be a template, resolved when a conversation with the agent starts.

applicableScopes.description:
ApplicableScopes is where a conversation with this agent may be created, and so where it works. E.g. ["tenant", "workspace"] lists the agent on the tenant and workspace AI pages and accepts a conversation at either; a conversation created anywhere else is refused.

An agent whose tools need a workspace lists workspace (or environment) and gets one on every run, because the conversation's own workspace is the one its `wf` commands, plans and deployments use.

enumDocs.description: Allows a conversation with this agent at the tenant.
Allows a conversation with this agent in a workspace.
Allows a conversation with this agent in an environment.

suggestedRoles.description: SuggestedRoles names the roles a tenant should grant this agent so its tools can act. An agent runs as itself, so a tool that reads the estate is denied unless the agent holds a role that allows it. The author declares what it needs here (e.g. ["viewer"] for a read-only agent); the agent's Access tab surfaces them. Each must be a role a tenant user can grant.

userPromptTemplate.description: UserPromptTemplate is an optional template used to build the prompt sent to the model. The values available to it depend on the context the agent is given.

defaultModel.description:
DefaultModel is the model this agent runs on, and how it should be tuned.

It names one model at one AIProvider, as "anthropic:haiku-4.5" for a provider named "anthropic" or "my-gateway:haiku-4.5" for one you define yourself. Naming the provider is what makes an agent portable: point it at a different provider offering the same model name and the agent runs there instead, with nothing else changed.

model.description:
Model names one model at one provider, as "<provider>:<model>" — for example "anthropic:haiku-4.5". The model part is the provider's portable model name, not an upstream model identifier.

A plain name looks for a provider of that name belonging to your tenant, and falls back to the Wayfinder-provided provider of the same name when you have defined none. So an agent shipped naming "anthropic:haiku-4.5" runs on Wayfinder's inference until you define your own "anthropic" provider offering that model, at which point it runs on yours instead.

Prefix the provider to pin it: "wayfinder/anthropic:haiku-4.5" always means Wayfinder's own, "myworkspace/gateway:haiku-4.5" a workspace-scoped one.

modelParameters.description: ModelParameters are the parameters to use for this model. Keys and values are provider-specific.

effort.description:
Effort is how hard the model should think before answering, from "none" for a straight answer through to "max" for the deepest reasoning.

It says what you want, not how to ask for it: models express reasoning depth differently — some take a level, older ones take a number of tokens — and the provider's catalogue translates this into whatever its model expects. That is what lets the same agent run on any of them. A level the model cannot reach is clamped to the nearest it can, so asking for more than a model offers is never an error.

Leave it unset to use the default the provider records for the model.

enumDocs.description: Answers directly, without reasoning first.
Does a little reasoning — for short, scoped tasks where speed matters more than depth.
Balances reasoning depth against time and cost.
Reasons thoroughly — the right default for work where the answer's quality matters.
Reasons harder than high, for demanding coding and agentic work on models that offer the level.
Reasons as deeply as the model can, for problems where correctness matters more than what it costs.

disablePromptCaching.description:
DisablePromptCaching turns off provider-side prompt caching for this agent.

Caching is on by default: the large context an agent repeats across turns — its tools and system prompt, then the conversation tail — is read back at a fraction of the input-token cost, which is almost always what you want. Turn it off only if you have a reason to. Anthropic dialect only, including its Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry backends; ignored by dialects that do not support it.

systemTools.description: SystemTools lists the built-in Wayfinder tools available to every conversation with this agent, in addition to the tools listed below — e.g. ["submit_result"] to let this agent finish its work with a result.

items.description: SystemTool selects one of Wayfinder's built-in tools for an agent to use.

name.description: Name is the built-in tool's name, e.g. "submit_result".

restrictedTo.description: RestrictedTo narrows what the tool may be used for. Its meaning depends on the tool, but is _typically_ the list of resource kinds it may get, list or write.

tools.description: Tools lists the tools this agent can call, each naming a registered tool and supplying any configuration that tool takes. Where a call runs — inside Wayfinder, or handed back to the client the user is chatting from — is decided by the tool itself, not here. The built-in submit_result tool is listed under systemTools instead.

items.description: AgentTool selects a tool for an agent to use, with any configuration that tool takes.

name.description: Name is the tool's registered name, e.g. "validate_resource".

config.description: Config is tool-specific configuration, as a JSON object the tool interprets.

mcps.description: MCPs lists the MCP servers this agent uses, each with the subset of that server's tools the agent may call. Each entry references an MCP by a scope-aware reference: a built-in agent must use "wayfinder/NAME", because it ships with Wayfinder and cannot know a tenant's MCPs; a tenant's own agent may use a bare "NAME" for one of its own MCPs, or "wayfinder/NAME" for one shipped with Wayfinder. The other direction — a tenant's own MCP reaching a built-in agent it cannot edit — is expressed on the MCP, in its spec.builtInAgents.

items.description: AIAgentMCPBinding gives an agent access to one MCP server and limits which of that server's tools it may call. It is the agent side of the binding between an agent and an MCP; the MCP side, its spec.builtInAgents, lets a tenant's own MCP reach a built-in agent it cannot edit.

mcp.description: MCP is the scope-aware reference to the MCP server this binding exposes to the agent: "wayfinder/NAME" for one shipped with Wayfinder, a bare "NAME" for one of the tenant's own. A built-in agent may only reference "wayfinder/NAME".

toolScope.description: ToolScope selects whether the agent receives every tool the MCP server advertises ("all") or only the subset listed in tools ("selected"). An empty value is treated as "all".

enumDocs.description: Exposes every tool the MCP server advertises to the bound agent. It is the default when ToolScope is unset.
Exposes only the tools named in the binding's Tools list to the bound agent.

tools.description: Tools is the list of the server's tool names the agent may call. It applies only when toolScope is "selected", and must be empty when it is "all". A name the server no longer advertises is ignored.

inputs.description:
Inputs are the values this agent calls the MCP with, for the inputs the MCP declares. They take precedence over the MCP's own, so one MCP serves many agents instead of a copy per agent, each pointed at a different account.

This is also how an agent avoids a hardcoded credential. A value may read the agent's own inputs, e.g. "${{ .Inputs.ddCredential }}", so the identity comes from whoever starts the conversation — one they hold at their own workspace or environment and are permitted to use — rather than one baked into the agent that the caller may have no access to.

Whoever supplies an identity is checked against their own grant: a literal named here is checked when the agent is saved, a value supplied by a conversation when that conversation starts, and the resolved credential again when the call is made, so a grant withdrawn in between stops working.

items.description: TemplatedInput is a named input value, potentially containing template expressions.

name.description: Name matches a ValueDefinition on the associated plan.

value.description: Value is a literal value or template expression, resolved at reconciliation time. Stored as json.RawMessage so non-string types (numbers, bools) survive YAML round-trips without forced quoting. Template expressions like "${{ .Vars.x }}" are stored as JSON strings.

resultSchema.description: ResultSchema declares the shape of the result this agent submits when it finishes its work, and how that result is validated and packaged for the caller.

kind.description: Kind is the Wayfinder resource kind the agent produces, e.g. "CloudResourcePlan". When set, the plan field is shaped by that kind's spec and the resource the agent generates is validated against the kind's own rules.

planSchemaType.description: PlanSchemaType names a built-in schema for a result that is not a Wayfinder resource — for example the contents of a Wayfinder.yaml. It shapes the plan field only: nothing is constructed or validated as a resource.

dataType.description: DataType references a DataType whose spec.schema becomes the JSON Schema for the plan field of submit_result. A bare name is the tenant's shared type, e.g. "incident"; "workspace/name" is one that workspace defined for itself, e.g. "team-a/incident", and only this agent's own workspace may be named — a tenant-scoped agent can use the shared types alone, and no agent can reach into another workspace. It is the tenant-authorable alternative to kind and planSchemaType — which name platform-owned schemas a tenant cannot define — and is mutually exclusive with both. A system-scoped agent cannot set it, having no tenant to resolve it in. A DataType whose schema is empty is allowed and leaves the plan field unvalidated (untyped).

immutableFields.description: ImmutableFields defines fields that must not be modified from the base spec. Checked before dry-run validation.

items.description: ImmutableField names a field of the resource an agent is authoring that it must not change from the value it started with.

path.description: Path is the dot-separated JSON path within the spec (e.g., "scope", "terraform.modules").

message.description: Message is the error returned to the agent if it changes this field.

preconditions.description: Preconditions are checked before accepting a "generated" result.

items.description: ResultPrecondition is a condition that must hold before an agent's result is accepted.

storeKeyExists.description: StoreKeyExists requires that the agent recorded a value under this key during the conversation, e.g. "state/test-passed" to insist that it tested its work before submitting it.

message.description: Message is the validation error message shown if the precondition fails.

resultField.description: ResultField is the JSON field name containing the result type ("generated"/"failed"). Defaults to "result".

responseField.description: ResponseField is the JSON field name containing the user-facing message. Defaults to "responseToUser".

warningsField.description: WarningsField is the JSON field name containing warning messages. Defaults to "warnings".

planField.description: PlanField is the JSON field name containing the resource spec to construct/validate. Defaults to "plan". Used when kind or planSchemaType is set.

submitResultDescription.description: SubmitResultDescription describes to the agent what the output should comprise.

resultOutputs.description: ResultOutputs declares what to do with the agent's result once the user accepts it: the files to write, and the pull request to open against the repository the conversation is working on. Ignored when the conversation is working on local files, which the CLI writes itself.

repoFiles.description: RepoFiles declares the files to commit to the repository, each projecting a field of the result onto a templated repository path. At least one entry is needed for there to be anything to propose.

items.description: RepoFileOutput declares one repository file written from an agent's result.

path.description: Path is the repository-relative path to write the file to. Supports Go text/template expansion against the sourceContext — e.g. "{{ if .subdirectory }}{{ .subdirectory }}/{{ end }}Wayfinder.yaml". After rendering, the path is re-checked against the conversation's subdirectory sandbox: it may not be absolute and may not escape the subdirectory root via ".." segments.

fromField.description: FromField is the key within the agent's result whose value becomes the file's content. It must name a top-level key; nested paths are not accepted.

format.description:
Format optionally specifies how to encode the extracted value:
  - "yaml" (default for object/map values) — marshals via YAML
  - "json"                                 — marshals via JSON with indent
  - "raw"                                  — string value written as-is
If empty and the value is a string, "raw" is used; otherwise "yaml".

prTitle.description: PRTitle is the template for the pull request title. When empty, Wayfinder uses a terse default derived from the agent's name.

prBody.description: PRBody is the template for the pull request body, which the provider interprets as Markdown. Rendered bodies are never logged — they may carry repository content the agent read.

commitMessage.description: CommitMessage is the template for the commit message, expanded against the same values as the title and body. Defaults to a terse "AI-generated <purpose>" when empty.

suggestedFileName.description: SuggestedFileName, when set, marks this agent's output as a document the user takes away (e.g. "Wayfinder.yaml") rather than a Wayfinder resource or an interactive shortlist. The result's plan field is then offered as a proposed document under this file name, which clients render uniformly (copy / download in the UI, write-to-disk in the CLI). Leave empty for resource outputs and search-style results.

agentDescription.description: AgentDescription describes what this agent does, so it can be listed to users.

description.description: Description says what this agent does, for a person choosing between agents, e.g. "Tests cloud resource plans". Keep it to a sentence or two: it is what a card and a list show.

userInputsNeeded.description: UserInputsNeeded lists what information a caller should gather before starting a conversation with this agent.

example.description: Example shows a typical use of this agent.

inputs.description:
Inputs declares what a conversation with this agent must supply, each with its name, type and whether it is required. A conversation whose spec.context does not match is rejected when it is created.

An input of type externalidentity asks for a credential rather than a value, which is what lets a shipped agent be given the identity it needs instead of naming one. Such an input is usually passed on to an MCP the agent binds, as a value in that binding's own inputs.

items.description: ValueDefinition defines the shape of an input/output/data value

name.description: Name of the variable

description.description: Description iof the value

secret.description: Secret indicates if the value is a secret and should be protected

type.description: Type is the type of the value

enumDocs.description: Is a string type
Is a number type (integer or floating point)
Is a boolean type
Is a list type of strings
Is a list type of numbers
Is a list type of booleans
Is a map type of strings
Is a map type of numbers
Is a map type of booleans
Is an arbitrary JSON type, used to represent any complex input/output that isn't better represented by the other types. Note that no validation is possible for a plain JSON input.

Is a reference to an ExternalIdentity, naming the credential an outbound call authenticates with. The value is the identity's name and the scope it lives at ("my-identity", "my-workspace/my-identity" or "my-workspace/my-env/my-identity"), never credential material itself. Supplying a value resolves it: the identity must exist, you must be allowed to use it for what is calling, and its own kind must be one the definition's identityTypes accepts. A value naming an identity that fails any of those is refused when it is supplied, rather than failing when the call runs. It may only be declared where a definition is able to load an identity. It is refused on a CloudResourcePlan's inputs and outputs, a KubeResourcePlan's inputs, a stack definition's vars, an IntegrationDefinition's paramDefs, and a repo template's inputs, all of which would otherwise receive the reference as a plain string.

Is a reference to a CodeRepo, naming the repository an AI agent works on. The value names the repository as its provider does, "github.com/OWNER/REPO" (e.g. "github.com/appvia/wayfinder"), never a URL or a git credential. Use it on an AI agent's input where the repository is not fixed when the agent is written: the input sets how much of the repository the agent needs (repoAccess) and the branch prefix for its changes (repoBranchPrefix), and whoever starts the conversation supplies the repository. The conversation's spec.sourceContext is built from the value they supply. Supplying a value resolves it: the repository must exist, and the grant in its usableBy must cover the access the input asks for. That grant is checked against the person supplying the repository, not against whoever wrote the agent. The agent is checked separately, against the same repository, when the conversation is created. It may only be declared where a definition is able to load a repository and check that grant. It is refused on a CloudResourcePlan's and a KubeResourcePlan's inputs and outputs, a stack definition's vars, an IntegrationDefinition's paramDefs, and a repo template's inputs: each of those passes its values through as text to Terraform, a Helm chart, a rendered manifest or a scaffolded file, where the reference is only a plain string and no grant over the repository is checked.

optional.description: Optional is true when no value need be supplied: the object declaring it can be saved, and switched on where it has a switch, without one. An unanswered optional value reads as its defaultValue when one is set, and as nothing otherwise. Whether whoever uses the object may supply it later is for that object to say.

minimum.description: Minimum is the minimum numerical value of the variable if a number/float

maximum.description: Maximum is the maximum numerical value of the variable if a number/float

minLength.description: MinLength is the minimum number or length of the variable if a string

maxLength.description: MaxLength is the maximum number or length of the variable if a string

minItems.description: MinItems is the minimum number of items in the variable if a list or map

maxItems.description: MaxItems is the maximum number of items in the variable if a list or map

pattern.description: Pattern is the pattern of the variable if a string. For list(string) and map(string), this is applied to each individual value in the list or map.

enum.description: Enum is the list of valid values for a string or number (or the values of lists/maps of those types). Ignored for other types.

requiredKeys.description: RequiredKeys is the list of required keys for a map variable. Ignored for other types.

refType.description: RefType describes that this value is a reference to another Wayfinder resource. When set, the value is validated to be the name of an existing resource of the given kind, optionally filtered by field constraints.

kind.description: Kind is the Wayfinder resource kind being referenced (e.g. "ExternalIdentity", "CodeRepo")

filter.description: Filter is an optional set of dot-path field matchers on the referenced resource. Keys are dot-paths (e.g. "spec.cloud"), values are the expected string match. All entries must match (AND semantics).

identityTypes.description: IdentityTypes lists the ExternalIdentity types this input accepts, e.g. ["BearerToken"] for an API that authenticates with a bearer token, or ["BasicAuth", "BearerToken"] where either will do. A value naming an identity of any other type is refused when it is supplied, rather than failing when the call runs. Leaving it empty accepts any identity type that can authenticate an outbound call. It may be set only on type=externalidentity, and is refused on every other type.

repoAccess.description: RepoAccess is how much of the repository the agent needs: "read" to clone and read it, "propose" to also commit to a fresh branch and open a pull request, or "proposeWorkflows" to also change the repository's CI workflow definitions. When empty, Wayfinder uses "read". Whoever supplies a repository must themselves be granted at least this much of it, and so must the agent, or the conversation is refused when it is created. It may be set only on type=coderepo, and is refused on every other type.

repoBranchPrefix.description: RepoBranchPrefix is prepended to the name of the branch the agent's changes are committed to, e.g. "wayfinder-ai/cost-control/". When empty, branches are prefixed "wayfinder-ai/". Set it so branch protection or CODEOWNERS rules in the repository match every branch this agent opens; whoever starts the conversation cannot change it. It may be set only on type=coderepo, and is refused on every other type.

schema.description: Schema provides additional guidance as to the shape of the value when type=json.

builtIn.description:
BuiltIn marks a shipped agent that Wayfinder's own features are built on — the testers, the assistant. It is meaningful only on a system-scoped agent, and it is what tells the two kinds of shipped agent apart.

A built-in agent is listed and usable as it stands. It has to be: the plan builders and the CLI call it by name, and putting an install step in front of it would put one in front of building a plan.

Every other published agent is an extra you install. It is offered in the catalogue, does not appear among the agents a tenant can talk to, and becomes usable once the tenant installs its own copy and configures it — which is the shape for an agent needing a credential nobody can supply on their behalf. Installing is the default because that is the ordinary case: the built-in set is small, fixed, and ours.

enabled.description:
Enabled toggles whether this agent can be used. Omitted means enabled — an explicit false is required to turn an agent off, so every agent that predates the toggle keeps working. Agents installed from the catalogue start disabled; turn them on once configured.

Turning one on is checked: every MCP it binds must exist and be enabled, which in turn required their integrations to be enabled. Its inputs are NOT checked here — those are answered per conversation and refused there.

relatesToConfig.description: RelatesToConfig constrains the resource a conversation with this agent may be about, named in the conversation's spec.relatesTo. When unset, a conversation with this agent cannot name a related resource.

required.description: Required indicates that conversations MUST specify a relatesTo resource.

allowedKinds.description: AllowedKinds restricts which resource kinds can be referenced by relatesTo. If empty, any kind is allowed.

prePopulateConversationStore.description: PrePopulateConversationStore lists which parts of the related resource are read and given to the agent when the conversation starts, so it does not have to fetch them itself. Any of "spec", "status" and "metadata".

validation.description: Validation defines field-level assertions on the related resource that are checked when creating a conversation. If any assertion fails, the conversation is rejected.

items.description: RelatesToFieldValidation defines a field-level assertion on the related resource.

field.description: Field is the dot-separated JSON path within the resource (e.g., "status.validationError", "spec.cloud").

mustBeNull.description: MustBeNull requires the field to be null, absent, or an empty value.

mustNotBeNull.description: MustNotBeNull requires the field to be present and non-null.

mustEqual.description: MustEqual requires the field to equal this exact JSON value.

message.description: Message is the validation error message shown if the assertion fails.

sourceRequirements.description: SourceRequirements states what repository a conversation with this agent must be given, so an agent that exists to change code says so up front. When unset, a conversation needs no repository.

requireSourceContext.description: RequireSourceContext indicates conversations must specify a sourceContext. When true, creating a conversation without spec.sourceContext is rejected. Defaults to false.

requireSourceAccess.description:
RequireSourceAccess states the least repository access a conversation must be given for this agent to be able to do its job, so an agent that exists to change a repository says so up front instead of failing partway through with a refusal the user cannot act on.

It is a MINIMUM on a ladder: "propose" is satisfied by a context that may also change workflows, and "proposeWorkflows" is what an agent that sets up or repairs CI should state. Setting it implies requireSourceContext — there is no way to satisfy a repository access requirement without a repository — so an agent need not set both.

enumDocs.description: Reads the repository and changes nothing.
Additionally commits to a fresh branch and opens a pull request — a source context whose propose is set.
Additionally changes CI workflow definitions — a source context whose propose sets allowWorkflows.

memories.description:
Memories is the list of durable note stores this agent keeps, each of which it sees as a directory under /memory that survives the conversation. Declaring one is all that is needed: the store is created the first time an agent needs it, so nothing has to be set up in advance.

Two agents that declare the same name at the same scope share one store, which is how one agent can record what another reads.

items.description:
AIAgentMemory declares one durable note store an agent keeps for itself, so a later run can build on what an earlier one found.

Describe what to keep in it, and how, in the agent's systemPrompt: the agent is told the store exists and where it is mounted, but not what it is for.

name.description: Name is the store's name, and the directory the agent sees it at — "run-ledger" is mounted at /memory/run-ledger. Two agents naming the same store at the same scope share it.

access.description: Access is how much of the store this agent gets: Write to record into it, Read to consult it without being able to change it. Defaults to Read, so an agent that does not ask to write cannot.

enumDocs.description: Mounts the memory read-only. An agent that only needs to consult prior notes should be given this: it cannot then corrupt a ledger another agent maintains.
Mounts the memory writable, so the agent can record what it learned for the next run.

scope.description:
Scope is the level the store is kept at, relative to where the agent runs: Tenant for one store shared everywhere, Workspace for one per workspace, Environment for one per environment. Defaults to Tenant.

A store kept per workspace or per environment needs spec.applicableScopes to include workspace or environment — otherwise every conversation with this agent is at the tenant, where the store has no home.

enumDocs.description: Keeps one memory for the whole tenant, shared by every conversation with this agent wherever it runs.
Keeps a separate memory per workspace, so what an agent learns about one workspace is not mixed with another. The agent must require a workspace (spec.scopeConfig.requireWorkspace).
Keeps a separate memory per environment. The agent must require an environment (spec.scopeConfig.requireEnvironment).

requiresCloud.description: RequiresCloud indicates that an AIContext targeting this agent must specify a concrete cloud. UIs use this to gate the cloud picker when authoring a context. Built-in cloud agents (the CloudResourcePlan editor/tester) set this; tenant-defined agents declare it for themselves — it is the only place a custom agent can express the requirement.

supportsAutonomous.description: SupportsAutonomous declares that this agent is safe to run hands-off, with no interactive user available to answer questions — the way a workflow task runs it. It is the author's promise that the agent can reach a conclusion on its own (typically a one-shot agent with a resultSchema that finishes via submit_result). It is checked when the agent is saved: an agent that sets this may expose no tool only a client can answer (e.g. suggest_ui_action), because a hands-off run has no client to answer such a call and would wait forever. Only such an agent may be referenced by a workflow "ai/agent" task.

supportsFollowPullRequests.description: SupportsFollowPullRequests declares that this agent goes on working on a pull request after opening it, rather than finishing at the pull request. It is the author's promise that the agent can pick the work up again from a comment or a review someone left there: told only that something was said, it reads the pull request itself and decides what to do about it, which is something its instructions have to cover. Only such an agent may be used by a conversation whose propose grant sets followPullRequest.

maxModelTurns.description: MaxModelTurns bounds how many model turns this agent may take in one uninterrupted stretch of work: each turn is one call to the model, which may use tools, and the agent keeps taking turns until it finishes, needs something it cannot get on its own, or hits this bound — at which point the conversation fails. Raise it for an agent with a lot of ground to cover (a deep investigation across many tools), lower it to cap what a single stretch can spend. The bound resets whenever the conversation continues after a pause — a reply, a client tool result, or a resource it was waiting for — so it limits one stretch of work, not the conversation's lifetime. Defaults to 20 when unset.

sandbox.description: Sandbox gives this agent a dedicated virtual machine to run commands in, and says what it needs from it. A tool that runs in the sandbox, such as bash, can only be given to an agent whose sandbox is enabled, and an enabled sandbox needs at least one such tool.

enabled.description: Enabled gives this agent a sandbox. When false, the rest of this is ignored and the agent has no machine.

persistence.description:
Persistence is whether the files this agent writes on its machine are still there after a break. Required when the sandbox is enabled.

oneTime keeps nothing: after a break the next command runs on a new, empty machine and the agent is told its files have gone. It starts faster and costs nothing while unused. Right for workflow tasks and agents that finish in one go.

resumable keeps the agent's working files through a break, so an agent picked up again finds its clones, installed packages and work in progress where it left them. Starting again takes a little longer, and the files are kept for a day after the conversation was last used, then removed. Right for conversations a person comes back to.

enumDocs.description: Keeps nothing through a break.
Keeps the agent's working files through a break.

storage.description: Storage is how much a resumable sandbox keeps for this agent, as a size such as "10Gi": its working files and, with full control, what it installs and the container images it pulls and builds. Leave it empty for Wayfinder's default of 5Gi; at most 20Gi. Only a resumable sandbox can be given storage.

size.description: Size is how much CPU, memory and disk this agent's machine is given, by name: one of the sizes Wayfinder offers, e.g. "S", "M" or "L". Leave it empty for the smallest, S, which is right for an agent that runs wf commands, git, kubectl, the cloud CLIs and small tofu plans. Choose M for large repositories, tofu plans over large stacks, and npm or go builds; L for docker builds, test suites and heavy compiles. An agent with full control that builds or runs containers usually wants M or L, though a single light `docker run` fits in S. A command that needs more memory than its size gives is stopped, and the agent is told why.

fullControl.description: FullControl gives this agent administrator access inside its own sandbox: it can install system packages with `sudo apt-get install`, and build and run containers with `docker build`, `docker run` and `docker compose`. On a resumable sandbox what it installs and the images it pulls and builds are kept with its files. The sandbox is still a dedicated virtual machine, and it still reaches only the hosts it is allowed. Leave it off for an agent that only runs commands: its sandbox then starts with fewer permissions. Full control does not change the sandbox's size: one that runs docker usually needs a larger size than the default. Where full control is not available, an agent asking for it is refused.

egress.description: Egress is what this agent's machine may reach on the network. Left out, it reaches what Wayfinder allows every sandbox.

allow.description: Allow lists the hosts the machine may reach over HTTPS and HTTP, e.g. registry.npmjs.org. A name starting with "*." covers that domain and every name under it, so *.example.com covers example.com and api.example.com. Addresses and ports cannot be allowed: only HTTPS on port 443 and HTTP on port 80 leave the machine.

replaceDefaults.description: ReplaceDefaults makes Allow the whole of what the machine may reach, besides Wayfinder itself, in place of the hosts Wayfinder allows every sandbox. Set it for an agent whose work needs only a few known hosts, so that nothing else it is talked into can reach anywhere. Defaults to false: Allow adds to those hosts.

directCloudAccess.description:
DirectCloudAccess states that this agent wields cloud credentials itself: the cloud CLIs on its machine run as the external identities it is granted, rather than Wayfinder using an identity on the agent's behalf.

Every external identity granted "directaccess" to this agent at the tenant, at the conversation's workspace or at its environment is written onto the machine as a profile named after that identity. An agent that sets this and is granted none of them where a conversation is being started is refused when it is created, rather than failing on the first cloud command it runs.

kinds.description:
AIContext is a piece of reusable background knowledge you write once and give to AI agents: your own standards, conventions and hard-won details that an agent could not work out for itself. It is markdown you author, plus the kinds of resource it applies to and, where relevant, which cloud it is specific to.

A context marked "Always" is given to every conversation about a resource of one of its kinds — a conversation with the assistant about a CloudResourcePlan, say, or with one of your agents about the resource it relates to — when its cloud matches. Wayfinder adds it, and nobody starting the conversation can leave it out. A conversation that is given a context starts with its whole body already in the agent's instructions, pinned at the version given, so what the agent was told does not change under it if the context is later edited. Contexts can be held at tenant, workspace or environment scope, so a team can add its own on top of the tenant's. The UI calls them "Agent Context".

A context is the opposite of a memory: you write a context and give it to an agent; an agent writes a memory for itself.

spec.description: AIContextSpec defines the content of an AI context, which kinds of resource it applies to, and how readily it is applied.

description.description: Description is a short summary of what this context provides, e.g. "Our naming and tagging standards for AWS". It is shown beside the name in lists, so you can see what a context is for without opening it.

markdown.description: Markdown is the body of the context. When a conversation is given the context, the whole body is added to the agent's instructions as the conversation starts.

cloud.description: Cloud optionally scopes this context to one cloud provider. When set, the context applies only to a conversation about a resource for that cloud, such as a CloudResourcePlan whose cloud is "aws". A resource with no cloud of its own is given the context whatever it says here.

forKinds.description: ForKinds lists the kinds of resource this context applies to, such as "CloudResourcePlan" or "KubeResourcePlan". A conversation about a resource of one of these kinds, with the assistant or with any agent, is given the context when its use is "Always". Only list a kind the whole body is genuinely useful for — a context has one body, not a section per kind. Each entry must be a kind of resource you write as configuration.

use.description: Use declares how readily this context is applied. "Always" gives it to every conversation about a resource of one of its kinds. "ByDefault" and "WhenChosen" are only offered where a person picks contexts for a run, such as the plan tester, pre-selected or not. An unset or unrecognised value is treated as "WhenChosen", so a context is never silently made mandatory.

enumDocs.description: Means the context is given to every conversation about a resource of one of its kinds, and cannot be left out.
Means the context is pre-selected where a person picks contexts for a run, such as the plan tester, and can be deselected there. It is never given to a conversation automatically.
Means the context is given only when a person picks it for a run, such as the plan tester. This is also what an unset or unrecognised value means.

kinds.description:
AIProvider declares where inference comes from, which models it can run, and what they cost. One provider is one place plus the key that opens it: a dialect (the wire format), a backend (the transport and credential) and a catalogue of models under portable names.

Wayfinder ships system-scoped providers, referenced as "wayfinder/NAME"; tenants may define their own at tenant, workspace or environment scope. An AIAgent selects one model at one provider through an AIModelRef such as "wayfinder/anthropic:haiku-4.5".

spec.description: AIProviderSpec configures one source of inference.

displayName.description: DisplayName is the human-readable name shown in the UI.

description.description: Description explains what this provider is for.

dialect.description: Dialect is the wire format this provider speaks, which decides how requests to it are shaped. A gateway that presents an Anthropic-shaped endpoint takes dialect "anthropic" however it routes upstream.

enumDocs.description: Is the Anthropic Messages API wire format.
Is the Google Gemini generateContent wire format.

Is the OpenAI Chat Completions wire format, at "/chat/completions" beneath the backend's base URL. It reaches OpenAI itself and the great many services that present the same shape — OpenRouter, LiteLLM, vLLM, Azure AI Foundry, Vertex AI's OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

backend.description: Backend is how Wayfinder reaches this provider and which credential opens it.

type.description: Type is the transport used to reach the provider.

enumDocs.description: Reaches the provider over plain HTTPS at its own base URL, authenticating with the headers its ExternalIdentity carries. This covers the vendor's own API and any gateway that fronts it — OpenRouter, LiteLLM, Azure API Management.
Reaches the provider through AWS Bedrock, signing requests with SigV4.
Reaches the provider through Google Vertex AI.
Reaches the provider through Azure Foundry.

baseURL.description:
BaseURL is the endpoint to send requests to, for a "direct" backend. Leave it unset to use the dialect's own public API; set it to route through a gateway such as OpenRouter, LiteLLM or Azure API Management.
